title: We Tested the Best Robotic Pool Cleaners of 2026: Beatbot, iGarden, and Dreame
summary:
Swimming pools are fun; cleaning them is not. That's the simple logic that drove WIRED's pool robot reviewer to spend four years testing the latest robotic pool cleaners. The market has shifted from pressure-side cleaners that rely on water pressure to battery-powered robots that can be dropped in and forgotten—at least for a while.

The top pick is the Beatbot AquaSense 2 Ultra. This 29-pound behemoth cleans floors, walls, and the waterline with near-perfect precision. Its battery lasts six hours underwater, and it even skims the surface. When finished, it floats, making retrieval easy. The downsides? It's unwieldy and costs around $3,000. For those on a budget, the Beatbot Sora 70 at $1,499 covers most of the same ground.

For lazy pool owners, the iGarden M1-AI is a game-changer. Its massive 12,500 mAh battery allows up to nine hours of floor-only cleaning, meaning you can leave it in the pool for up to three weeks. Its racecar-inspired red design is a bonus. Meanwhile, the Dreame Z1 Pro, originally $1,499, has seen dramatic price cuts to $499. It's slower and less thorough, but its sensors map your pool, and a magnetic charging cable keeps water away from electronics. It's the best value for casual cleanups.

Whether you want top-tier performance or a budget-friendly helper, there's a robot for every pool.
why_it_matters: Robotic pool cleaners show how consumer robots are moving beyond vacuums and lawn mowers into specialized outdoor chores, raising questions about cost, battery life, and whether automation is worth it for ordinary households.

background_read: WIRED (a technology magazine that tests consumer gadgets) has tracked robotic pool cleaners for four years, a period in which the category shifted from machines plugged into a pool's main pump system toward standalone battery-powered robots.

Older pressure-side cleaners relied on water pressure from the pool's pump and used long hoses connected to a wall fitting, which could tangle and made setup more awkward than simply dropping a robot in the water.
Beatbot and Dreame are part of a newer wave of appliance makers applying robot-vacuum navigation, sensors, and rechargeable batteries to outdoor pool cleaning.
Because pools vary widely in shape, size, and debris load, reviewers separate premium flagships that scrub walls and waterlines from budget models that mainly handle floors and simpler cleanups.

The main trade-off in testing is now between price, battery capacity, and cleaning thoroughness, so a chart-topping model can coexist with a cheap casual cleaner that still solves the basic chore for many pool owners.

perspectives.description: Owners save time and avoid the unpleasant chore of manual pool cleaning. A battery-powered robot can work daily without hoses, walls, or constant attention.
Premium models like the Beatbot AquaSense 2 Ultra cost thousands of dollars and are heavy, so not every household can justify them. Cheaper models may lack full coverage or thoroughness.
The shift from pressure-side to battery-powered robots mirrors what happened with indoor robot vacuums, as sensors, mapping, and rechargeable batteries made small autonomous devices more practical.
As sensors and mapping improve, pool robots could become even more independent and drop-in-and-forget. The next years may bring lower prices, better battery life, and smarter cleaning paths.
